title: Supernova Eventos
summary: A prototype of an internal events micro-app I built at Tsoft for Telefónica: employees discover events, sign up and show a pass with a QR code; organizers create events step by step, choose the audience and check people in. It runs entirely in the browser, with fictional data and no backend.

facts.v: Built the prototype, already as a mid-level dev

tldr.v: Bring together discovering internal events, signing up with per-session capacity, the entry pass, and audiences and invitations.
A catalog that orders itself by schedule, sign-up with a pass and QR code, and a step-by-step creator for organizers; set in a 3D universe that never holds an action back.
A prototype with fictional data and local storage. No backend, SSO or email sending: the backend contract was written down as a proposal.

p: A micro-app for a large company's employees to find internal events, sign up and get in with a pass. I built it at Tsoft for Telefónica, already as a mid-level (Ssr) developer, as a prototype: it runs entirely in the browser on fictional data.
list: Employee: searches and filters the catalog, saves favourites, signs up for a session with guests and gets a pass with a QR code, a calendar and an .ics file.
Organizer: creates events step by step (details, audience, email template and review), exports sign-ups and checks people in by reading the QR code.
Three presentations of the same app, with the same data: a classic one, a navigable 3D universe and a hybrid one, with illustrations on 3D planes.

p: The employee and the organizer use the same app and the same saved data. What one publishes shows up in the other's catalog, and one's pass is what the other validates at the door.

diagram.title: From the catalog to the door
diagram.caption: A prototype with fictional data: everything is saved in the browser. The admin view can be explored, but it isn't real authorization.

catalog.label: Catalog
catalog.note: Active, upcoming and finished, in that order, three per page. It reorders itself when an event starts or ends.

signup.label: Sign-up
signup.note: Each session has its own capacity; guests and terms are optional. Synchronous guards prevent booking or cancelling twice.

create.label: Event creator
create.note: Details, audience, email template and review. The draft saves itself, including when the tab closes. Once published, the event appears for its audience.

invite.label: Invitation
invite.note: The audience can be the whole company, a pick from a fictional staff list, or an imported Excel or CSV file. The preview is personalized and sends nothing.

checkin.h: Checking someone in with a QR code
p: This is where the prototype decides whether someone gets in, so validation is strict even without a server.

seq.title: From the camera to the check-in
seq.caption: A QR code alone never grants entry: it is always checked against a saved booking. When the browser supports it, the check-in runs under a lock (Web Locks), so two tabs can't record the same entry.

p: A React SPA built with Vite and published on GitHub Pages, with no backend. The three presentations share the same app, the same flow controller and the same storage.

diagram.title: One app, three presentations, one state
diagram.caption: Everything runs in the browser. CI only installs, builds with type checks and publishes.

html.label: Initial HTML
html.note: The orbital scene is already in the HTML, with critical CSS; React and the intro carry it on with the same clock. There is no logo-only splash screen.

app.label: Events app
app.note: No business operation waits for an animation to finish.

lazy.label: On demand
lazy.note: The GSAP intro, the QR code library and the Excel reader download separately, when needed. The classic presentation never downloads Three.js.

universe.label: 3D universe
universe.note: It lives outside views and dialogs. Each command carries an increasing ID: a new journey cancels the previous one. It never writes data.

security.h: Security and privacy in a prototype
p: Without a server there is no real security to show. What there is: care with data, and honesty about what's missing.

items.t: No real authorization, and it says so
items.d: Interface permissions are for the demo; final authorization belongs to a server. localStorage can be edited from the browser, so it is not a source of authority.

items.t: A QR code with the minimum
items.d: The pass carries only demo identifiers: names, emails and audiences never go into the QR code. The pass JSON is not a secure token.
Excel or CSV up to 5 MB and 5,000 rows, with required columns, validated emails and duplicate detection. A CSV with unclosed quotes is rejected.
It is requested only after an explicit action, with a message for each kind of error. On a phone it needs HTTPS.
example.com and .test domains. The README asks not to load real employee data.
Actions pinned by SHA, no secrets, and only the permissions needed to publish.

items.t: The first frame doesn't wait for React
items.why: The orbital scene is already in the HTML with critical CSS, and the GSAP intro carries it on with the same clock. A build script keeps the HTML and the intro in sync.

items.t: One Canvas that never holds the app back
items.why: The universe lives outside the views and takes commands with an increasing ID. Signing up or checking someone in never waits for an animation, and if the download, a shader or the WebGL context fails, a static backdrop remains and the actions keep working.

items.t: Pay for 3D only when it's seen
items.why: It pauses off-screen, when the tab is hidden or from My profile; the mouse doesn't move the camera; pixel density is capped and the hybrid version trims stars if the device is slow. The repo's docs record median frames of 16 ms in local Chrome on integrated graphics, and note that this isn't sustained FPS. I didn't measure it again.
Per-event sessions are optional: an old booking without a session falls into the main session, and the migration keeps the events the user created.

The repo documents the contract it would need: idempotency keys, expected revision, atomic booking, cancellation and check-in, and an opaque or signed token per booking instead of the demo's QR code. And it forbids inventing endpoints as if they existed.
With Codex, in separate roles for the front end and for the trailer, each with its own files. The 3D universe came out of a pack of three prompts, implemented and checked locally.

p: This prototype's quality lives in end-to-end journeys and visual QA, not in unit tests: it has none.

status.h: Status, and what I don't claim
list: A prototype built at Tsoft for Telefónica, with fictional data and local storage.
There is no backend, SSO, real staff list, email sending, cross-device capacity control or authorization.
It isn't in production and there are no usage metrics: capacities and sign-ups are sample numbers.
The demo's QR code isn't a secure token: in production a server would have to issue and validate it.
I didn't check that the three presentations open from their own URL in the published version.
I don't describe Telefónica's internal systems, processes or data.
